items.prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if some node can be reached again by following next pointers. Use O(1) extra memory.
items.why: Cycle detection on a linked list with O(1) space → Floyd: a 2-step hare must meet a 1-step tortoise inside any loop. A visited set works but costs O(n).

items.prompt: Given a sorted array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
items.why: Sorted array + a pair condition → two pointers moving inward from both ends. Both pointers move by one at different ends; nothing is chasing anything.

items.prompt: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes between positions left and right and return the new head.
items.why: The task is to rewire next pointers backwards → in-place reversal. Fast/slow only finds positions; it doesn't flip links.

items.prompt: An array of n + 1 integers holds values in 1..n, so at least one value repeats. Find it without modifying the array and with O(1) extra space.
items.why: Read-only + O(1) space rules out cyclic sort (it swaps) and a hash set (O(n)). Treat i → nums[i] as a next-pointer: the duplicate is the entry of a cycle, found with Floyd.

items.prompt: An array of n integers holds values in 1..n; some appear twice. Return every value that appears twice. You may modify the array.
items.why: Values in 1..n, all duplicates wanted, mutation allowed → cyclic sort: put each value at its index, then the misplaced ones are the duplicates. Floyd finds only one duplicate.

items.prompt: Starting from n, repeatedly replace the number with the sum of the squares of its digits. Return whether the process reaches 1, using O(1) extra memory.
items.why: An implicit next-function that must either hit 1 or loop forever → cycle detection on the sequence. The digit maths is only the next-function. A seen-set would work but costs O(n) memory, so O(1) means Floyd.

items.prompt: Given an array of integers and k, return true if two equal values sit at most k indices apart.
items.why: 'At most k apart' is a contiguous window of size k + 1 → keep a set of the last k values (sliding window). There's no cycle or middle to find.

items.prompt: Given the head of a linked list, remove the k-th node from the end in a single pass and return the head.
items.why: k-th from the end of a singly linked list in one pass, without knowing the length → two pointers on the same list, one with a k-node head start. Dummy-head splicing (linked-list basics) only handles the removal. The one-pass position comes from the pointer pair.
